beats: Hook: the same blur filter, two programs: a few lines on one card vs a fat hand-tuned binder that runs many times faster (line_sched_card_vs_binder, line_sched_blur_frames).
The kernel explosion: many models x many chips = too many kernels to hand-write; the 'black magic' in the middle (line_kernel_pile_coder, line_heap).
Image processing hit it first: many filters x many devices; Halide (PLDI 2013) splits the program in two (line_sched_blur_frames).
Algorithm vs schedule: the recipe says WHAT the dish is, the kitchen plan says HOW (split, order, parallel); any plan gives the same dish (line_sched_recipe_and_plan, line_sched_same_cake).
Schedule primitives: tile, vectorize, parallel: cut the sheet into squares and hand them out (line_sched_dough_tiles).
Autotuning: generate many plans, time each one, keep the fastest (line_sched_stopwatch_trials, line_knob_board for the search space, line_tally_pages).
Halide's payoff: less code, faster, portable: the algorithm never mentions the hardware (line_sched_many_kitchens).

To tensors: Tensor Comprehensions (2018) applies the idea to matrix math; TVM (OSDI 2018) adds graph-level moves (fusion, layout) and template-free tuning; one model, many chips (line_sched_many_kitchens).
Fusion, the graph-level move: do not put the chopped onions back in the fridge (line_sched_onion_trips vs line_sched_onion_fused).
Takeaway: keep what and how apart; let a search find the how.
